First off, shop sales. If you have an Aldi anywhere near you, go there. If not, Wal-Mart or store generic brand.

Lean protein, fruit, vegetables.

Meats: Chicken and Fish will be your friends. Usually dark meat is cheaper, like chicken thighs and legs. Tilapia is a mild and usually inexpensive fish as it is farmed, not caught.

Buy the sale fruits and vegetables as they are ususally in season. Don't get too fancy at first! Carrots, onion, tomato, potatoes, sweet potatoes, broccoli, green beans. For fruits, apples, oranges, grapes, nectarines are in season now too.

Invest in some spices such as onion powder, garlic powder, cumin, paprika, poultry seasoning, Italian seasoning, parsley, chili powder, salt, and pepper. You can do a ton of different things with spices and you won't feel like you are eating the same thing. GENERIC EVERYTHING. Don't fall into the organic fancy bottled/packaged bullshit it's a trap for stupid people. I take that partly back, organic is fine just don't pay a shitton for it.

Breakfast: Eggs, whole grain bread, peanut butter, yogurt, milk, granola, oatmeal or cereal. Stay away from overly processed food like pop tarts as they don't have a lot of nutrition. Look for 5 grams protein, 5 grams fiber.

Snack: Granola bars, I like nature valley. Again, no processed shit. Those chewy ones covered in chocolate stay on the shelf. Fruits, washed and sliced. Get fancy and make a fruit salad if you want. Trail mix, make your own with nuts, grains, coconut, chocolate chips, dried fruits. Cheese cubes, get the block and slice it yourself. I paid for the pre-cubed and was disappointed. Crackers, whole grain like Triscuits. Summer sausage if you can afford.

Lunch: Whole grain bread, sandwich meat, cheese, mayo, mustard. Leftovers if you have them. Chips, generic. Although there is no substitute for Lays chips, I'm sorry. More fruit. Carrot sticks.

Dinner: Lean protein, easily prepared. Season it up and gently cook it so you don't burn the shit out of it. Fish cooks very fast and will taste like shit if done wrong, you want juices running clear and the fish to flake easily. Have a starch, potatoes are easy to bake or mash. I like pasta mixes for the week, it's too hard for me to make something from scratch all the time. Pasta Roni is our favorite brand, usually on BOGO too. More vegetables!! That shit is good for you. Steam them, roast them in the oven, dress them up with spices or a little grated cheese. Rice is economical and filling but high in carbs so not something to eat every night. Beans are filling and good, but make your own. Don't buy that shit like pork and beans in a can, that's fucking nasty.

Baking mixes are fine, I recommend the Martha white mixes for 1 person because they are good, and cheap.

Make sure you have the basic pantry staples. A little oil, some baking spray, tin foil. Flour, sugar, baking powder, baking soda. Bread crumbs, seasonings, dry pasta, pasta sauce for emergencies, soup when you feel sick. Milk, butter, eggs, cheese for dairy.

Make sure you have the basics for cookware. Buy cheap now, upgrade later. Pots and baking sheets, nothing fancy. Most of what I make is with 1 cookie sheet, 1 cutting board, measuring cups, 2 pots, 2 skillets.

I love helping bachelors eat healthy! I just sat down with a bachelor friend the other day and gave him advice on a healthy menu and grocery list for himself.

On the weekend, do some prep work. Some ideas:

  • Pick a rotisserie chicken off the bones and put the meat into a tupperware container (use the bones and fat to make stock with veggie trimmings, if you're so inclined). Put some chicken on salads, make fajitas, eat it with beans and rice, do whatever you want with it, but this way it's already cooked and easy to take out however much you want to add to your meal.

  • Boil 6-12 eggs, depending on how many you would eat/day (perfect boiled eggs: eggs in pot + cold water to cover, put lid on pot, put on stove and turn on high, when it reaches a boil, leave it on the burner and turn the stove off and set timer to 13 minutes. When the timer goes off, drain hot water, put eggs in ice water, then easily peel after 5 minutes, store eggs in a baggie and use through the week). With the work out of the way, you can eat eggs with bacon or ham in the morning, make egg salad for lunch, add to lentil curry pouches, add to beans and rice, chop it up and add to leafy salads.

  • Chop fruit up into a big fruit salad, put into small tupperwares for work lunches or eat after work for something sweet but not processed sugar; in-season sale fruit can be chopped and frozen in bags for additions to breakfast protein smoothies (my usual breakfast).

  • Chop veggie sticks and put into snack bags for easy snacks with guac, peanut butter, or hummus.

  • Drain cans of tuna, add chopped celery or baby bok choy (Koreatown will sell this), make a tuna salad (eat on romaine lettuce leaves is my recommendation).

  • Cook a pork shoulder (also called pork "butt") in the slow cooker with a dry chili rub, onions, garlic, and some stock and apple cider vinegar on low for about 8 or so hours. Shred it up into a container and eat it throughout the week. Use it in tacos, rice bowls, sandwiches; it will last a single man a very long time. I like to make curtido (cabbage, carrots, onion, apple cider vinegar, brown sugar, salt, hot pepper flakes) to eat with my pulled pork; curtido keeps very well in the fridge too, deepening with flavor each day.

  • Make a meaty veggie casserole on Sunday and eat a square of it each day for lunch or dinner. I just made a casserole that had sliced eggplant on the bottom (you could also do zucchini, carrots, whatever you like), a sauteed mixture of ground turkey, onion, red bell pepper (you could also add spinach, beans, corn), fried and chopped bacon, and crushed tomatoes and spices in the middle, then spiralized (you could slice it) sweet potatoes on top. Made a gravy with almond meal and almond milk and poured that on top. Was delicious and full of protein, veggies, and fiber! The whole 11" x 13" casserole probably cost me less than $10 and made 18 square-piece servings to feed four people two dinners, and had at least 3 adult lunches left over. If you don't mind eating the same thing for a few days in a row (or you don't mind freezing portions and re-heating them later), then casseroles can save you a lot of money.

  • Tacos/taco bowls are easy and healthy dinners during the busy workweek. Shred some lettuce, chop some tomatoes, make that curtido, grate your cheese, (cook rice if you don't eat flour or corn tortillas), prep whatever meat you want to use (the pulled pork, rotisserie chicken, or even frozen fish sticks) and have everything ready in tupperwares at the beginning of the week to let you easily put together some tacos after work for dinner.

There are other things that you can do, but I'm not sure what kind of calorie or nutrition requirements you have or need or foods that you avoid. Salads for lunch are the easiest thing--and that's what I send with my husband every day. Spinach, matchstick carrots, chickpeas, chopped egg, chopped chicken, alfalfa sprouts, cucumber slices, cherry tomatoes; he adds sunflower seeds and a balsamic dressing that he keeps in his desk at work. Otherwise for dinner, if you do some basic prep work over the weekend (easily while watching a movie on a tablet on the kitchen counter), you won't have much to do during the week.

Congrats on your new job, and I hope you meet your future wife soon!
